title: Systems assessment, neurological observations and chest auscultation
blurb: Score the GCS correctly, know when neurological observations demand urgent review, and interpret what you hear in the chest.
question: Mr Kerrigan, 45, is on a surgical ward after a head injury. His GCS was E4 V5 M6 at 14:00. At 14:30 and again at 15:00 it is E4 V5 M5. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: A systems assessment works through the body in a fixed order so nothing is missed: respiratory, circulatory, neurological, musculoskeletal and skin. For each system you look, listen and feel, and compare left with right. Formally it is a structured physical examination that turns observations into findings. In plain English: you are asking each system 'are you coping?', and writing down the answer in a way the next person can compare.
teach.cite: NMC proficiencies Annexe B 2.7; RCUK ABCDE approach

head: Component
Responses and scores
rows: Spontaneous 4 · To sound 3 · To pressure 2 · None 1
Obeys 6 · Localising 5 · Normal flexion 4 · Abnormal flexion 3 · Extension 2 · None 1
teach.caption: Total 3 (no response) to 15. Score the best response seen. Record NT (not testable) if, for example, swollen eyes or an endotracheal tube prevent a response.

teach.h: Record the parts, not just the total
teach.body: NICE NG232 says base monitoring and handover on the three separate responses: a GCS of 13 is recorded as E4 V4 M5, and the components always accompany the total (13 out of 15), never the total alone. Two people with a total of 13 can be very different. Use a standardised stimulus when a response to sound is absent: fingertip pressure, trapezius pinch or pressure at the supraorbital notch. NICE says give more weight to a 1-point fall in the motor score than to the same fall in eye or verbal response.
teach.cite: NICE NG232 recs 1.3.1–1.3.3 and 1.9.13; Teasdale GCS aid (2015)

rows.label: Levels
values: Alert, new Confusion, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive

rows.label: NEWS2 score
values: C, V, P or U all score 3

teach.caption: RCUK: in the D of ABCDE, use ACVPU or the GCS, check pupils and measure blood glucose.

teach.h: Neuro observations after admission for head injury
teach.caption: Minimum set (NICE NG232): GCS, pupil size and reactivity, limb movements, RR, HR, BP, temperature and SpO2. If someone deteriorates later, go back to half-hourly and restart the schedule.

teach.h: Signs that need urgent reassessment by a doctor

children.label: Eye or verbal down 3+, motor down 2+
Unequal pupils, limb or face asymmetry

teach.caption: Ask a second competent colleague to confirm at once if possible. If no one is available, contact the supervising doctor without waiting (rec 1.9.14).

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Kerrigan's falling motor score
items: 14:00: E4 V5 M6 = 15. 14:30: E4 V5 M5 = 14, he now localises to pressure instead of obeying commands.
15:00: still E4 V5 M5. A 1-point drop has lasted at least 30 minutes, and it is in the motor score, which NICE says to weigh more heavily.
The nurse checks his pupils (size, equality, reaction to light) and limb movements, then asks a colleague to confirm the GCS straight away.
She calls the supervising doctor for urgent reassessment using SBAR, reporting E4 V5 M5 and the time of change, and restarts half-hourly observations.

teach.h: What you hear in the chest (RCUK ABCDE)
head: Finding
Suggests
teach.caption: Listen with the person sitting up where possible, compare left and right at matching points, front and back. Stridor is an emergency: get expert help immediately.

teach.body: Capillary refill time: press a fingertip held at heart level for 5 seconds; normal is usually under 2 seconds, and a longer time suggests poor perfusion (RCUK). Check limb temperature, colour and pulses. Look at the skin over pressure areas: if erythema does not blanch, start pressure ulcer prevention and recheck at least every 2 hours (NICE CG179). Note limb power and any new weakness on one side.

teach.text: The lowest GCS is 3, not 0, and the maximum motor score is 6, not 5. Do not write 'GCS 13/15' and move on: record E, V and M separately, because a 1-point motor fall matters more than a 1-point verbal fall.

items: GCS: E4 V5 M6, total 3–15; record the three parts (NICE NG232).
Head injury obs: half-hourly until GCS 15, then half-hourly 2 h, hourly 4 h, 2-hourly.
Urgent reassessment: sustained 1-point drop, motor down 2, eye or verbal down 3, unequal pupils, agitation, worsening headache or vomiting.
Stridor or wheeze = partial airway obstruction; bronchial breathing = consolidation; crackles with raised JVP = fluid overload.
CRT: 5 seconds' pressure at heart level, normal under 2 seconds.

summary: You can now carry out a structured systems assessment, score and record the GCS by its three components, follow NICE NG232 observation frequencies and triggers for urgent review, and interpret common chest sounds. You know which findings mean calling for help now.

A.q: Mrs Okafor's eyes open when the nurse speaks to her. She talks in sentences but does not know where she is, and she localises to trapezius pinch. What is her GCS?
A.why: Eyes open to sound = E3; coherent but not orientated = confused, V4; localising = M5. Total 12, recorded as E3 V4 M5 (NICE NG232).

whyNot.1: Opening to speech is 'to sound', E3; E2 is opening only to pressure.
whyNot.2: Localising is M5; M6 needs her to obey a command.
whyNot.3: Coherent sentences while disorientated is 'confused', V4; V3 is single intelligible words.

A.q: During an ABCDE assessment the nurse hears a harsh, high-pitched noise on inspiration. According to RCUK, what does this most likely indicate?
options: Pleural fluid at the lung base
A.why: This is stridor. RCUK states that stridor or wheeze suggests partial but significant airway obstruction, a medical emergency needing expert help immediately.

whyNot.0: Consolidation with open airways gives bronchial breathing on auscultation, not inspiratory stridor.
whyNot.1: Fluid overload gives crackles, often with a raised JVP, not stridor.
whyNot.3: Pleural fluid reduces breath sounds and gives a dull percussion note.

A.q: Ms Ali, 34, is admitted for head injury observation. Her GCS is 15 after assessment in the emergency department. What is the minimum frequency of neurological observations for the first 2 hours?
A.why: NICE NG232: for a GCS of 15, observe half-hourly for 2 hours, then hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly.

whyNot.0: Every 15 minutes is more often than the NICE minimum for someone with a GCS of 15.
whyNot.1: Hourly observations come after the first 2 half-hourly hours.
whyNot.2: 2-hourly is the frequency reached only after 6 hours of closer observation.

B.q: Mr Kerr, 58, was E4 V5 M6 after a head injury. For the last 40 minutes he has been E4 V5 M5, confirmed by a second nurse. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask the supervising doctor to reassess him urgently
Record it, as a 1-point fall is normal variation
Wait for a 2-point fall before escalating
B.why: NICE NG232 rec 1.9.13: a sustained (at least 30 minutes) drop of 1 point needs urgent reassessment by the supervising doctor, with more weight given to a fall in the motor score.

whyNot.0: Observation alone is not enough; a sustained 1-point fall is a trigger for urgent medical reassessment.
whyNot.2: NICE treats a sustained 1-point fall as deterioration, not variation, especially in the motor score.
whyNot.3: A 2-point motor fall is an immediate trigger, but a sustained 1-point fall already meets the criteria.

B.q: How should the nurse measure capillary refill time in an adult during an ABCDE assessment?
options: Press a fingertip at heart level for 5 seconds
Press the nail bed for 1 second, hand lowered
Press a toe for 5 seconds with the leg raised
Press the earlobe for 10 seconds, head tilted
B.why: RCUK: apply pressure for 5 seconds on a fingertip held at heart level (or just above), enough to cause blanching, then time the return of colour; normal is usually under 2 seconds.

whyNot.1: One second is too short to blanch reliably, and a lowered hand fills faster, giving a falsely normal result.
whyNot.2: Raising the leg changes refill; RCUK describes the fingertip at heart level.
whyNot.3: The earlobe is not the site RCUK describes, and 10 seconds is not the standard pressure time.

B.q: Mr Fox, 81, is two days after surgery and has had several litres of IV fluid. He is now breathless with a raised jugular venous pressure. Which chest finding best supports fluid overload?
B.why: RCUK lists dyspnoea, raised JVP, a third heart sound and pulmonary crackles as signs of cardiac failure; if they appear during fluids, the rate should be reduced or stopped and help sought.

whyNot.0: Stridor suggests upper airway obstruction, not fluid in the lungs.
whyNot.2: One-sided absent sounds suggest pneumothorax, pleural fluid or a blocked airway.
whyNot.3: Bronchial breathing over one area suggests consolidation such as pneumonia.

C.q: Mr Barnes, 77, takes apixaban and fell 3 hours ago. His GCS remains 15, but his left pupil is now larger than his right and he has vomited twice. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue hourly observations as his GCS is 15
Give an antiemetic and recheck pupils in 2 hours
Request urgent reassessment by the doctor
Dim the lights and recheck pupil size later
C.why: NICE NG232: new or evolving signs such as pupil inequality, and persistent vomiting, need urgent reassessment by the supervising doctor even if the GCS is unchanged. Anticoagulation adds to his risk.

whyNot.0: A normal GCS does not cancel new pupil inequality and vomiting, which are separate triggers.
whyNot.1: Treating the vomiting and waiting 2 hours delays the assessment that NICE requires now.
whyNot.3: Pupil inequality is a sign of possible deterioration, not a lighting problem to recheck later.

C.q: A nurse finds that a patient's motor score has fallen from M6 to M4. No other competent colleague is free to confirm the finding. What should she do?
options: Contact the supervising doctor straight away
Wait for a colleague to confirm before calling
Repeat the GCS herself after 30 minutes
Document it and hand over to the next shift
C.why: A motor fall of 2 or more points needs urgent reassessment. NICE NG232 rec 1.9.14: get confirmation immediately if possible; if no one is available, contact the supervising doctor without it.

whyNot.1: Confirmation must not delay escalation; NICE says contact the doctor if no one can confirm.
whyNot.2: Waiting 30 minutes applies to deciding whether a 1-point drop is sustained, not to a 2-point motor fall.
whyNot.3: Handing over without escalation leaves a serious deterioration unmanaged.

C.q: Which handover entry best follows NICE NG232 for reporting a head-injured patient's conscious level?
C.why: NICE NG232 recs 1.3.1–1.3.3: base monitoring and exchange of information on the three separate responses, for example E4 V4 M5, give the total out of 15 and always accompany it with the components; the time lets changes be compared.

whyNot.0: A total out of 15 hides which component has changed.
whyNot.1: ACVPU is too coarse for head injury observations; NICE uses the GCS components.
whyNot.2: A total without components loses detail, and 'alert' conflicts with V4 confusion.

reteach.title: Think of the GCS as three dials
reteach.question: Instead of one number, picture three dials: eyes, voice and movement. Which dial moving should worry you most?

blocks.body: The eye dial runs 1–4, the voice dial 1–5 and the movement dial 1–6. Add them for a total of 3–15, but always report each dial (E4 V4 M5). The movement dial is the most telling: a 1-point fall in motor response deserves more weight than the same fall elsewhere, and a 2-point motor fall triggers urgent review at once.

items.label: a 1-point drop lasting this long needs review
eye or verbal points down: urgent review

blocks.text: 'Confused' (V4) means talking in sentences but disorientated; 'Words' (V3) means single intelligible words. Do not mix them up.

explain.body: Eyes: spontaneous 4, to sound 3, to pressure 2, none 1. Verbal: orientated 5, confused 4, words 3, sounds 2, none 1. Motor: obeys 6, localising 5, normal flexion 4, abnormal flexion 3, extension 2, none 1.

test.q: What is the highest possible score for the motor component of the GCS?
test.why: Best motor response runs from 1 (none) to 6 (obeys commands).

whyNot.0: 4 is the maximum for eye opening.
whyNot.1: 5 is the maximum for verbal response.
whyNot.3: 15 is the maximum total GCS, not the motor component.

explain.body: Alert, new Confusion, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive. On NEWS2, anything other than Alert scores 3. It is fast but coarse; the GCS picks up smaller changes.

test.q: Mrs Dale, 80, was alert yesterday. Today she is talking but newly disorientated. How is this recorded on ACVPU and NEWS2?
test.why: New confusion is C on ACVPU and scores 3 on NEWS2.

whyNot.0: She is not alert in the ACVPU sense because the confusion is new.
whyNot.3: She responds and talks spontaneously, so this is C, and V would also score 3, not 2.

explain.body: NICE NG232: agitation or abnormal behaviour; a 1-point GCS drop sustained for 30 minutes; any drop of 3 or more in eye or verbal, or 2 or more in motor; severe or increasing headache or persistent vomiting; new pupil inequality or limb or facial asymmetry.

test.q: Which change on its own is enough to trigger urgent reassessment under NICE NG232?
options: Verbal score falling by 1 for 10 minutes
Eye score falling by 1 for 15 minutes
Heart rate rising by 10 per minute
test.why: Any drop of 2 or more points in the motor score triggers urgent reassessment.

whyNot.0: A 1-point fall needs to be sustained for at least 30 minutes to trigger review.
whyNot.1: A 1-point eye fall must last at least 30 minutes; eye or verbal falls of 3 trigger at once.
whyNot.2: A small heart rate rise is not one of the NG232 neurological triggers.

explain.body: Stridor or wheeze: partial airway obstruction. Rattling: secretions. Bronchial breathing: consolidation. Absent or reduced: pneumothorax, fluid or blocked consolidation. Crackles with raised JVP: fluid overload.

test.q: On auscultation, bronchial breathing is heard over the right lower lobe. What does this most likely indicate?
test.why: RCUK: bronchial breathing indicates lung consolidation with patent airways, such as pneumonia.

whyNot.0: Partial upper airway obstruction causes stridor or wheeze.
whyNot.2: Pneumothorax gives absent or reduced sounds and hyper-resonance.
